Can extreme heat affect your mental health?
Another summer of extreme temperatures may be behind us, but researchers are continuing to learn more about how heat affects your mental health.
High temperatures have been linked with changes in mood, sleep and thinking as well as more serious mental health concerns.
“Heat puts stress on the body and brain,” says Dr. Jada Johnson, a psychiatrist at Advocate Medical Group Psychiatry. “When temperatures climb, people may have more trouble concentrating or managing emotions.”
How can extreme heat affect your mental health?
Extreme heat can disrupt sleep and make it harder to recover from everyday stress. As temperatures rise, you may notice changes such as:
For some people, the effects can be more serious. Extreme heat has also been associated with increases in aggression and substance use as well as symptoms of depression.
Who is most vulnerable?
Extreme heat can affect anyone, but some people may be more susceptible to its effects. That includes those who already have a mental health condition.
Certain medications, including some antidepressants and antipsychotics, also can make it harder for the body to regulate temperature. If you take one of those medications, continue taking it as prescribed and talk to your doctor if you have questions about staying safe in hot weather.
Another international study also found that sustained extreme heat was associated with an increased risk of hospitalization for mental health conditions. The association was particularly strong among older adults.
How can you protect your mental health during extreme heat?
Taking steps to stay physically safe in hot weather can help protect your mental health, too. Johnson recommends:
- Maintaining your normal sleep routine as much as possible
- Paying attention to changes in your mood or behavior
- Checking in on family members or friends who may be especially vulnerable
“Be aware of how you’re feeling during periods of extreme heat,” she says. “If you notice significant or persistent changes in your mood, thinking or behavior, talk to your doctor or a mental health professional.”

Akola: A cobra coiled inside the toilet commode caused anxious moments for a family in Akola’s Sudhir Colony on Sunday night. The family was relieved after the venomous reptile was safely rescued by wildlife department warden Bal Kalane and wildlife rescuer Satish Buddhivaparkar.The incident took place at around 10 pm on Nov 1 at the residence of the Kandekar family. As per Kalane, snake sightings generally decline during Nov. “However, water scarcity this year is affecting the natural habitats of reptiles too. Snakes and other reptiles are increasingly compelled to move closer to villages and urban settlements for water, cooler surroundings and shelter,” he claimed.As per Kalane, sightings and rescue operations involving pythons have also been reported in several parts of Maharashtra over the past two months. “Pythons generally inhabit areas close to water bodies,” he said.Experts have advised citizens not to approach, handle or attempt to kill snakes if they are spotted inside houses. “People should maintain a safe distance and immediately contact trained snake rescuers or the forest department,” they said.

As temperatures rise amid concerns over the El Niño weather pattern, health experts have urged Nigerians to eat water-rich fruits and vegetables, drink plenty of water and limit exposure to direct sunlight to prevent heat-related illnesses.
The experts identified watermelon, oranges, cucumbers and pineapples as water-rich foods that can supplement fluid intake and help maintain adequate hydration during periods of extreme heat.
They also advised Nigerians to carry water bottles when going out.
Similarly, the experts advised farmers, traders, construction workers and other outdoor workers to schedule strenuous activities for the early morning or evening hours and avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight, particularly around midday.
In an interview with PUNCH Healthwise, a public health physician, Dr Rotimi Adesanya, said consuming fruits and vegetables such as watermelon, oranges, cucumber and pineapple could help people maintain hydration during periods of high temperatures.
He also urged Nigerians to recognise warning signs of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, protect vulnerable groups, including children and older people, and seek immediate medical attention when severe symptoms occur.
Adesanya, the Director of Medical Services at the Federal College of Education (Technical), Akoka, Lagos, gave the advice while outlining measures individuals could take to protect themselves from heat-related illnesses.
He advised Nigerians to include water-rich fruits and vegetables in their diets, saying, “Eat water-rich fruits and vegetables like watermelon, oranges, cucumber and pineapple.”
He also encouraged people to drink plenty of water and carry water bottles, particularly when going outdoors.
“Drink plenty of water: Always carry a water bottle,” he advised.
The physician urged people to avoid direct exposure to the sun during its strongest hours, recommending that they stay under trees or indoors between 11 am and 4 pm.
He also advised people to wear loose, light clothing, noting that cotton clothes could help the body stay cool.
Adesanya warned that dizziness and weakness could be early signs of heat exhaustion, urging people experiencing such symptoms to alert someone or seek help.
He identified confusion, fainting, hot, dry skin and collapse as warning signs of heatstroke, stressing the need for immediate action when they occur.
“Know the warning signs of heat stroke. The signs include confusion, fainting, dry hot skin, or collapse. In case of collapse, quickly move the person to shade, pour cool water, and seek medical help immediately,” he said.
He further advised Nigerians to check regularly on vulnerable people, particularly elderly relatives, babies and sick neighbours, noting that they required extra attention during periods of extreme heat.
“Never leave children and elderly alone in hot rooms. Check on them often,” he cautioned.
Adesanya also urged people living with hypertension, diabetes and heart conditions to monitor their health closely during hot weather.
He advised households to keep their homes cool by using fans, opening windows at night and covering windows during the day to reduce indoor heat.

Face-to-face classes suspended in Albay towns due to extreme heat
The mayors of Camalig and Guinobatan made the decision to suspend or recommend to school heads the suspension of classes due to prevailing high temperatures which could cause heatstroke.
NAGA CITY – In-person or face-to-face classes were suspended in the towns of Guinobatan and Camalig in Albay province beginning noontime Tuesday, 3 November, until due to the extreme heat.
In Guinobatan, Mayor Anna Gemma Ongjoco declared that face-to-face classes in all elementary and secondary schools, both private and public, were suspended starting 12 noon due to the recorded heat index of 37 degrees Celsius. All teaching and non-teaching personnel are advised to adopt a work-from-home arrangement.
Ongjoco based her decision of the Department of Education (DepEd) Order No. 64, series 2026.
DepEd uses the 4H framework to manage class schedules and learning modalities based on daily heat index and indoor temperature/humidity monitoring. The 4H framework stands for “HAYO” (below 27°C — manageable conditions) where standard face-to-face classes continue, supported by regular hydration breaks and cooling measures; “HINAY” (27°C – 32°C — caution) which calls for reduced face-to-face hours with hybrid or flexible learning arrangements; “HINGA” (33°C – 41°C — extreme caution/danger) which means suspension of physical, face-to-face classes, shifting to modular or remote learning tasks; and “HINTO” (over 42°C — extreme danger) which demands total suspension of all academic activities, both physical and home-based.

A new campaign launched by Wessex Water is helping customers identify and repair leaking toilets, which are often overlooked but can waste up to 400 litres of water each day.
The Big Leaky Loo Fix offers supply customers up to £50 towards the cost of fixing a leaky toilet, which could otherwise add £70 a month to water bills for those on a meter.
Aimee Shaw, head of customer engagement at Wessex Water, said: "Water trickling down the back of the toilet pan is often silent and can go unnoticed, but it’s simple to check using a piece of toilet paper and can usually be fixed relatively easily by replacing a broken flush or fill valve.
Wessex Water has launched a new campaign to help its customers find and fix leaky loos, offering up to £50 towards the cost of a repair. (Image: Wessex Water)
READ MORE: Dorset MP calls for Ofcom review for failing to regulate GB News and Royal Mail
"Our customers have made fantastic water-saving efforts this year, even before the hosepipe ban, and we know they will be eager to save more water and potentially money too by joining our Big Leaky Loo Fix.
"Working together to fix these leaks will help protect supplies, support the environment and reduce pressure on water resources while they recover."
Customers can claim the £50 by arranging a repair with a qualified plumber, paying for the work, and submitting the paid invoice to Wessex Water.
The company estimates that around 10 per cent of homes in its region have a leaking toilet.
Despite recent rainfall, parts of the region remain in severe drought, and the campaign aims to support water resource recovery following a dry summer and below-average reservoir levels.
Customers can also apply for a leak allowance after the repair, which offers a bill reduction to cover the cost of water lost through the leak.
Wessex Water introduced its first hosepipe ban in 50 years this August.
The company continues to focus on leak repairs and water-saving partnerships with high-use businesses as part of its drought response.
Wessex Water recommends using a plumber listed on the WaterSafe Register.
Customers can check for a leaky toilet by placing toilet paper at the back of the pan for three to four hours—if it becomes wet, a leak is likely.
For more information, visit the Wessex Water website.

Severe Cyclonic Storm Murasu continues to disrupt normal activities in south coastal Andhra Pradesh, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to issue a red alert for the state.
Heavy rainfall caused a delay of approximately two-and-a-half hours in the start of vote counting for urban local body elections in Vijayawada on Tuesday. Counting began with postal ballots, and the process is being conducted separately for the East, West, and Central constituencies in different halls.

In Guntur, the counting process has also been slowed due to adverse weather conditions. Across the NTR district, vote counting commenced at 8 am despite the rain, with electoral agents and staff arriving on time.
NTR District Collector Dr G Lakshmisha reported that the counting of votes for the five local bodies in the district was proceeding peacefully under police security. He stated, “The counting of votes for the local body elections is underway in the NTR district. In the entire district, the local body election counting process has started. We have five local bodies… Everything is going peacefully… Police security is in place everywhere… Everyone is cooperating… The spirit of the free and fair elections is upheld.”
The cyclone has severely impacted agriculture and allied activities, particularly in and around Ongole. Salt pans and fields have sustained extensive damage, with salt production adversely affected by heavy rains and strong winds, resulting in significant losses for farmers and salt pan workers.
Railway operations have also been disrupted. South Coast Railway’s Vijayawada Division issued a passenger advisory announcing the temporary suspension of train movement on the Vijayawada-Ongole-Gudur section following gale-force winds recorded at Karavadi Station. Train services on this route are regulated at originating and en-route stations, with 29 trains affected by regulation, cancellations, diversions, or rescheduling due to cyclone-related conditions.
Passengers have been urged to cooperate as railway authorities prioritise safety and apologise for any inconvenience caused.
The local body elections cover 92 urban local bodies across Andhra Pradesh, including 13 municipal corporations and 79 municipalities and Nagar Panchayats. Polling was held on November 1 from 7 am to 5 pm.

Hyderabad: Telangana is likely to see light rain and thunderstorms in several districts on November 3.
India Meteorological Department (IMD) has issued a yellow warning for 10 districts.
The weather activity comes as neighboring Andhra Pradesh faces heavy rainfall and strong winds under the influence of Severe Cyclonic Storm Murasu, which crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast early Tuesday.
According to the District Level Nowcast issued by the IMD Meteorological Centre, Hyderabad, at 7 am on November 3, light rain of around 5 mm per hour and light thunderstorms, accompanied by surface winds below 40 kmph, are likely in Bhadradri Kothagudem, Hanamkonda, Jangaon, Khammam, Mahabubabad, Medak, Mulugu, Nagarkurnool, Suryapet and Warangal districts.
Residents in the affected districts have been advised to remain alert and take necessary precautions during thunderstorms.
Cyclone Murasu brings heavy rain to Andhra Pradesh
Meanwhile, Andhra Pradesh is witnessing the impact of Cyclone Murasu, which crossed the south Andhra Pradesh coast between Nellore and Narsapur, close to Ongole in Prakasam district, between 3.30 am and 5.30 am on Tuesday.
The cyclone made landfall with sustained wind speeds of 100-110 kmph and gusts reaching 120 kmph, according to the IMD.

Bengaluru is set for a wet start to November, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issuing a yellow alert for heavy rain, thunderstorm, lightning and squalls over South Interior Karnataka from November 3 to November 5. The yellow category means residents should stay aware of changing conditions.
According to IMD's sub-division-wise warnings issued on November 3, the alert covers all three days, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Coastal Karnataka is under the same warning. North Interior Karnataka has only a thunderstorm and lightning alert for the same period, with no heavy rain flagged. From November 6 to November 9, IMD shows no warning for any of the three sub-divisions.
The weather department says mostly cloudy skies will be seen across Karnataka with occasional sunshine. Light to moderate rain is likely at isolated places across the state, while scattered showers are expected over the south interior and coastal regions between November 3 and November 5, with heavy rain possible at isolated spots. IMD has also said cold and fog are likely in many parts of the state during the night and morning hours, so early commuters may find visibility reduced.
In the city itself, the day began cloudy, with the temperature around 23°C. Forecast models put the maximum for Tuesday at about 28°C and the minimum near 20°C, with a 35% chance of rain. Wednesday looks similar, with a high of about 28°C, a low of around 20°C and the same 35% chance of rain. The chance of rain eases to 15% on Thursday, even though the IMD warning is in force through that day, which suggests that the heavy spells are likely to be patchy and localised, not citywide.
Bengaluru Weather Forecast for this weekend
The weekend looks largely dry. Rain chances stay between 15% and 20% from Friday to Sunday, with daytime temperatures easing from about 28°C to 26°C. Nights turn a little cooler, with the minimum dipping to nearly 19°C by Monday, November 9 and around 18°C by November 10, when the chance of rain falls to just 5%.
For Bengaluru, the usual cautions apply on rain days. Waterlogging at low-lying stretches and underpasses, slow-moving traffic during evening peak hours and poor visibility in the early morning fog are the main concerns. Commuters are advised to keep an eye on updates from IMD and the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC) and to plan travel around the showers.
